segments.text: enemies of the cross of Christ, whose end is destruction, whose God is their
appetite, and whose glory is in their shame, who set their minds on earthly
things.
For our citizenship is in heaven, from which also we eagerly wait for a
saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ, who will transform the body of our humble
state into conformity with the body of His glory, by the exertion of the
power that He has even to subject all things to Himself.
We considered last week the contrast that Paul is drawing here between those who
like Paul could present themselves as an example to the believers and those who
merely preach the right doctrine but whose lives were not an example.
One of the things that we see Paul stressing very strongly is the importance
of those who preach the Word as being examples to the flock.
And this is something that Peter says too in 1 Peter 5 about elders being an
example to the flock, 1 Peter 5.3.
And when Paul writes to Timothy, whom he had sent to Ephesus to help in the
church there, he tells him also in 1 Timothy chapter 4 and verse 12,
show yourself an example to those who believe.
And Paul himself was an example.
He could tell Timothy in 2 Timothy chapter 3, you have fully known my manner of
life and my teaching.
Second Timothy chapter 3 verse 10.
And he tells the Philippians 2, Philippians 3 17, brethren join in following my
example.
Our lives are not an example.
We have no authority from God to preach the Word to others.
We read about Jesus in Matthew chapter 7 and the last verse that the people
when they heard the Sermon on the Mount were amazed for he taught them as one
having authority, Matthew 7 29, not as the scribes.
Now what was it that gave Jesus this authority when he spoke the Word of God?
This authority came because Jesus had obeyed the Word.
We read in Acts 1 1, Luke says, the first account I composed, which is the
Gospel of Luke, about all that Jesus began to do first and then to teach.
He practiced and then he preached what he had already practiced.
He taught what he had already done.
Then he told people to be pure in heart because it was because he was already pure
in heart and it kept himself pure in heart for 30 years.
That's why what he spoke on the Sermon on the Mount had authority.
When we preach what has not become a reality in our lives, then we have no
authority from God.
We can have eloquence and we can impress people, but we have no spiritual authority.
Spiritual authority does not come nearly with the baptism in the Holy Spirit, but
because we live a life that corresponds to the Word we preach.
And that's why Paul could say, join in following my example.
But he said in Philippians 3 18, there are many on the other hand who walk as
enemies of the cross of Christ.
Now Paul did not speak about these enemies in a harsh way.
He says in Philippians 3 way 18, for many walk of whom I often told you and
now tell you even weeping.
In other words, as he was writing these words to the Philippians, he was weeping.
His heart was grieved that there were people who called themselves Christians, who were
preaching the Word, and yet whose lives were a contradiction to the way of the cross.
They were enemies of the cross in the sense that they had not chosen the way of
the cross.
They had not chosen to go into the death of Christ in their life.
If I do not choose to be conformed to his death, as Paul says in Philippians 3 10, then
I am an enemy of the cross.
Either I am a friend of the cross of Christ, or I am an enemy of the cross of Christ.
If I am a friend of the cross of Christ, I embrace the cross and die on it every day,
as Jesus calls me to in Luke 9 23, die to myself, my honor, my reputation, my desires,
my lust.
But if I am an enemy of the cross, I don't want to die, I want to preserve my self-life.
At the same time, I am in desire to have the honor of being one who preaches the Word.
Now, Paul spoke about such people with weeping, and when we speak about the enemies of the
cross of Christ, if there is a harshness in the way we speak, then we are not following
in the footsteps of Paul.
He spoke about them weeping.
He did expose them.
He was not one who would hide the truth, but like in the case of Jesus, there was grace
with the truth that manifested the glory of God in Paul's life, as it did in Jesus'
case.
Jesus wept over the city of Jerusalem.
Then he went into that city and chased out the money changes in the temple.
That's what we read in the Word of God, and this is what Paul did too.
He wept for the enemies of the cross of Christ, and then he exposed them, rootlessly.
Yes, but he had wept for them before.
Now in verse 19, we see something of what it is that makes, in specific terms, a man and
enemy of the cross, whose end is destruction.
That is obvious.
If a man preaches what he does not practice, it is very clear that his end will be destruction.
Jesus said in Matthew 23, concerning the Pharisees, Matthew 23 verse 3, He told His
disciples, all that the Pharisees tell you to do, tell you, do and observe.
Do what they tell you because their doctrine is right, but don't do according to their
deeds, because they say things and do not do them.
The Pharisees were people who preached something but did not practice it.
And to them, He said, woe unto you, Pharisees, how can you escape the sentence of hell?
Matthew 23 verse 33.
And so those who would preach something which they do not practice in their own life and
therefore have to tell people, don't look at me, but look at Jesus to escape the responsibility
of being an example, their end is destruction.
And their end will be a greater destruction than the destruction of those who have rejected
the gospel.
Certainly, for here are people who have not only rejected that life of Jesus, but dared
to talk about it and therefore add hypocrisy to all their other sins, whose end is destruction.
And it says here, their God is their appetite, that is, their belly is their God.
Their sensual desires are what they worship.
Now when a man desires to satisfy the lust of his body, he becomes an enemy of the cross
of Christ.
It can be in as simple a matter as eating, where eating can become a God in our life.
That's what it says here in verse 19.
Those whose stomachs have become their God, those who are fastidious and particular about
their tastes, those who are very careful and who are disturbed and offended and upset when
they do not get food according to their taste.
If I can get offended and upset over such a simple thing as food not being up to the mark,
whether it is at home prepared by my wife or in some other place, if it disturbs me,
it would indicate that my God is my stomach.
For after all, what is food and drink?
Only to enable us to survive.
And God would deliver us from this fastidiousness and particularity about taste in food by allowing
us to die.
We are not called to live in order to eat, but rather to eat in order to live.
It's not just in obviously sinful things like adultery and murder that we become the
enemies of the cross.
Those are very obvious areas.
It can be a very simple thing like the appetite for food, which we need to mortify.
Paul says in 1 Corinthians 6 about how he himself controlled himself in the matter of
appetite because he didn't want to become a slave to anything.
He says in 1 Corinthians 6.12, the middle of it, all things are lawful for me, but
I will not be mastered by anything.
What is for the stomach?
He says in the next verse, the stomach is for food.
1 Timothy 6.13, 1 Corinthians 6.13, but God will do away with both of them.
No, the body is for the Lord, and then the Lord is for the body.
We are to keep the desires of our body under control.
Otherwise, as Paul says in 1 Corinthians 9.27, we can preach to others and be disqualified
ourselves.
And that's what happened to the many people.
He speaks often in Philippians 3.18.
They preached to others, but they did not keep their bodily passions and desires for
food or sex or anything under control, and therefore they were disqualified as far as
God was concerned.
He turned now to Philippians 3.18.
For many walker whom I often told you and now tell you even weeping that they are enemies
of the cross of Christ, whose end is destruction, whose God is their appetite, and whose glory
is in their shame, who set their minds on earthly things, for our citizenship is in
heaven, from which also we eagerly wait for our Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, who will
transform the body of our humble state into conformity with the body of His glory, by
the exertion of the power that He has even to subject all things to Himself.
We saw last week something about what it means to be an enemy of the cross of Christ.
The end of such people is destruction, those who would proclaim the right doctrine but who
have no lives that they can point to as examples.
And their God is their stomach.
They live for their physical appetites.
They have not got their appetites under control.
And I mentioned how if we get offended, for example, over food that is not good tasting
or that disturbs us, that would indicate that in some measure our God is our belly,
that that means so much to us.
We have to allow the cross to do a work there so that we are freed from being
fastidious about food tastes.
And it says here their glory is in their shame, the things that they should be ashamed
of, their glory in.
To seek the honor of men, for example.
That is the thing a man should be utterly ashamed of.
And yet many Christians, their glory is in the fact that men think highly of them, sometimes
even worldly unconverted people.
Think, for example, to get honor in the eyes of unconverted people, an unconverted world
which crucified Jesus, to seek their honor or an unconverted religious Christendom, of
who have authority and position in Christendom, who are unconverted, as there are many today,
among bishops and archbishops, etc., to seek their honor.
That's a shameful thing.
And yet there are many people who glory in the fact that they have honor before these
people.
They are obviously enemies of the cross of Christ.
When we seek for honor from those who do not wholeheartedly follow Jesus, when we
seek for honor from created beings, then our glory is in our shame, the thing that we should
be ashamed of, the falsely glorying, and who set their minds on earthly things.
Here's another characteristic of those who are enemies of the cross of Christ.
Their God is their appetite, their glory in earthly honor, and then their mind is set
on earthly things, material things.
And the God of this world has allowed their mind to be occupied with these things.
Now it doesn't mean that they steal, it doesn't mean that they cheat anybody.
They may be quite upright in those matters, but their mind is perpetually preoccupied
with money and material things.
Now there are many Christian workers like that whose mind is always set on where they
can get gifts and where they can get money.
Now these are enemies of the cross of Christ.
How many recognize themselves to be enemies of the cross of Christ?
Because their mind is set on earthly things.
Now here are three things that we see in verse 19.
Our sensual appetites, earthly honor, and material things.
These are the three areas in which people go astray.
And people are led astray by the devil, and those who have not overcome their sensual
appetites, those who have not overcome the desire for honor from men, and those who
have not overcome preoccupation with material things and money, cannot be examples for others
to follow, cannot be true servants of the Lord.
Hereby you can distinguish a false prophet, that he is a slave to essential appetites,
either food or sex or something, that he seeks honor, that he speaks and does things
because he wants honor for himself.
And he is a slave.
He desires material things.
His mind is on money and material things, often, even if he doesn't cheat or steal.
These are the marks of enemies of the cross.
For where the cross does a work in slaying a man's self-life, he is not a slave to
his appetites.
He has overcome his sensual appetites.
He does not desire the honor of men, and he has overcome the lust for material things
that dwells in our flesh.
He goes on to say, But our citizenship is in heaven, from which we eagerly wait a savior
the Lord Jesus Christ.
Our citizenship is in heaven, therefore our mind is set on the things that are above.
Now this is the mark of those who can be an example, those who really belong to heaven
and who know it deep down in their mind so thoroughly, but their mind is therefore set
on the things that are above.
Now if we say that our citizenship is in heaven, but our mind is set on earthly things,
and we covet what somebody else has, and we are always thinking of material things and
how to make more money and how to get a little more and looking for gifts from other
people, then we are hypocrites.
For we cannot say that our citizenship is in heaven and have our mind set on the things
of earth, and think of those people who fight for money, or fight for property, or fight
for material things.
Jesus said to Pilate in John chapter 19, My kingdom is not of this world.
And if My kingdom were of this world, then My servants would fight, John chapter 18
and verse 36.
Now that's the good confession that Jesus made before Pontius Pilate.
My kingdom is not of this world.
And when Paul writes to Timothy, he says in 1 Timothy chapter 6 about this good confession.
1 Timothy 6, 12, he says, You made a good confession in the presence of many witnesses.
Now I charge you, he says, in 1 Timothy 6, 13, in the presence of God who gives life
to all things and of Christ Jesus, who testified the good confession before Pontius Pilate.
The same good confession which Timothy made was the one that Jesus made before Pontius
Pilate.
What was that good confession?
That My kingdom is not of this world.
That you keep the commandment without stain.
No, our kingdom does not belong to this world.
And therefore, we do not fight for anything material.
If a person would fight for our court, we'd let him have it, and our shirt too.
That is the attitude of the one who is following Jesus.
He does not fight for earthly things because his mind is not set on earthly things.
Those who are interested in these things are enemies of the cross.
Their citizenship has not yet been transferred from earth to heaven.
But Paul says, our citizenship is in heaven.
We belong to heaven.
And therefore, our interest is set on things there.
We're not interested in how much money we are going to make.
We believe that God is sovereign and He allows us to have enough for our needs on earth.
And that's all we desire in any case.
He says, when Jesus will come, verse 21, He will transform this body of our humble state
into conformity with the body of His glory.
Now the body that we have now is called the body of our humble state, or a lowly body.
In other words, a body in which the only legitimate thing we are permitted to do is
to humble ourselves.
The only thing that we can do in this body which is acceptable to God is to humble ourselves
in every situation.
That's why it's called the body of our humble state.
Jesus Himself, when He came in this body, we consider that earlier in Philippians 2.5-8
that He, though He existed in the form of God, gave up that equality and took upon Himself
the form of a man.
And as a man, He humbled Himself.
Why?
Because He took upon Himself a body of humiliation, a body in which the only thing that
He could do was to humble Himself.
He knew that.
And so all His days, He humbled Himself.
He did not judge others.
He said, I do not judge anyone, He said in John chapter 8.
No, when we judge others, we think that we have already got a glorified body.
There is a day coming when the saints will judge the angels and the world, but that
is when we have a body of glory.
Not now.
Now we have no right to judge anyone except ourselves.
That is to humble ourselves, to judge ourselves, not to be a busy body in other people's matters.
When we begin to interfere in other people's matters and pass opinions about other people,
even in our thoughts or pass judgments on them, we are sitting on the throne of God.
No.
Our body is a body of humble state.
One day, Jesus will transform it into a body of glory by the exertion of the power that
He has even to subject all things to Himself.
This is the hope that we have.
And blessed are those who recognize that this body which they carry around with them, with
a flesh in which dwells no good thing, demands that they humble themselves in every situation,
never seek their own, never exalt themselves.
It's completely and totally wrong to exalt ourselves or to seek honor as long as we
have this body of a humble state.
It's completely and totally wrong to judge others.
No.
Let us recognize that this body will one day be transformed, but until then, let us humble
ourselves and recognize that our citizenship is in heaven, seeking nothing on this earth,
and God will give us His glory in that coming day.
We turn now to Philippians chapter 4.
Therefore, my beloved brethren, whom I long to see, my joy and crown, so stand firm
in the Lord my beloved.
Whatever you read in Scripture, the word therefore, it means that it goes back to what was said
previously.
And in the previous verses, verses 17 to 21 of chapter 3, Paul had been speaking about
his own example and about those who were enemies of the cross of Christ because they
were slaves to their appetite or certain earthly honor or sought material things, and who did
not recognize that this body was a body of our humble state in which we were called to
be servants of everyone else.
And he says, in view of all this, if you recognize that this body is a body in which we are
called to be servants and to humble ourselves, chapter 3, 21, then stand firm in the Lord.
If you realize that in this body we are not to seek for earthly things because our
citizenship is in heaven, and when we get there the Lord will give us all things, including
a glorious body.
Then stand firm in the Lord, my beloved brethren, in view of all this.
If we really believe the doctrine that our citizenship is in heaven, our mind cannot
be set on earthly things.
It will be quite easy for us to stand firm in the Lord if we really deep down in our
heart believe that our citizenship is in heaven, that we are pilgrims and strangers on this
earth, that this body is a body of our humble state.
Now the other thing we notice in this verse is that Paul calls these Philippian Christians,

If we would follow in the example of Paul, then we would see that we need to look at
others in the church, others who are children of God as our joy.
And then he goes on to speak in verse 2 and 3 about two sisters who are not living in
harmony together.
Verse 2, �I urge Euryodia and I urge Syntychae to live in harmony, to be of the same mind
in the Lord.� Now here were two sisters, as far as we can understand.
In verse 3 it says, �These women shared in Paul�s struggle in the cause of the
gospel.� Now here were two women who were not just ordinary sisters in the church,
but who were people who worked together with Paul in the gospel.
They did not have any authority, or they did not teach men.
Paul never allowed such things as we read in 1 Timothy 2, but they did work together
with Paul for the furtherance of the gospel.
Maybe in counseling sisters, maybe in helping with the younger girls perhaps, or small
children, but in some way they worked together with Paul for the spread of the gospel in
Philippi.
But yet, though they were quite zealous in the work of the Lord and were co-workers
with Paul in the cause of the gospel, yet they could not get along with each other.
There was strife and contention.
It could possibly have come out of jealousy that one was doing a better work than the
other, or one had a gift that the other didn�t have, or something like that, or

Now Paul knew that wherever there is a disagreement like this, neither of the two parties actually

However two Christians, and particularly two Christian workers, disagree with each other.
There is no question of who is right or who is wrong.
As long as there is a disagreement and contention, the one who wins is always the devil, not
the one who wins the argument, for one can win the argument over the other, but it�s
the devil who wins the victory.
And so Paul knew that, and Paul knew that once the devil wins a victory by bringing
division or discord between two of God�s children, that then those two will have no
spiritual authority over satanic powers.
For Jesus said that two must agree if they are to receive anything from the Father.
Matthew 18, verse 18 to 20, that if we are to bind anything on earth that is to be bound
in heaven, then verse 19 of Matthew 18, two must agree, agree meaning they must be
in complete symphony, because then where two people who agree like that have gathered
together, Matthew 18 to 20, the Lord is in the midst.
Now when two people disagree, the Lord withdraws his presence.
He cannot be in the midst of contention and strife.
This is why it is very, very important that there be agreement between those particularly
who are in leadership or in Christian work.
And so Paul says, �I urge you, dear and senticly, to live in harmony in the Lord,
to really be of the same mind.
This is God's calling for us that we might be of the same mind.� When we studied Philippians
chapter 2 and we saw Paul speaking about being of the same mind in Philippians 2.2, we saw
in Philippians 2.3 that the two things that prevent us from being of the same mind
are selfishness and pride.
And it is absolutely certain that these two sisters could not be of the same mind because
of one or both of these reasons, selfishness and pride, seeking their own in some way, their
own gain, their own profit, or seeking their own honor.
Usually it is only one of these two things that cause contention, and the devil wins the
victory.
Paul knew this and so he urged them to be of one mind.
And he says in verse 3, �Indeed, true comrade, I ask you to help these women.
Help them to be of one mind.
Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called the sons of God, who have shared
my struggle in the cause of the gospel, together with Clement also and the rest of my fellow
workers whose names are in the book of life.� Paul had a number of fellow workers.
He mentions Clement and the other fellow workers that he had whose names were in the
book of life.
But among them were also these two women.

Now it is clear, as we have mentioned earlier from 1 Timothy chapter 2, concerning the place
of women in the ministry of the gospel, Paul says there are two things and does
not allow a woman to do.
In 1 Timothy 2 verse 12, �I do not allow a woman to teach or exercise authority over
a man.� These are two things that are forbidden to women, to teach men and to exercise authority
over men.
But yet Paul had women who worked together with him in the spread of the gospel.
And this is something that we must recognize that in the new covenant, the Holy Spirit
has been poured out upon God�s sons and daughters.
It is very clear from Acts chapter 2 when Peter quoted from Joel�s promise, he says,
�I will pour out my spirit upon all mankind and your sons and your daughters will prophesy.
And upon my bond slaves both men and women�, Acts 2.18, �I will pour out my spirit and
they will prophesy.� We read in Acts chapter 21 about Philip the evangelist, Acts 21.9,
who had four virgin daughters who were prophetesses.
We read in Romans chapter 16 about Phoebe, who was a servant of the church in St.
Croix.
And so we find that Paul, who never allowed a woman to teach men or to exercise authority
over men, yet had a number of women who were co-workers with him in other ways, for there
were many sisters to be counseled.
There was a lot of individual work to be done among the women.
And here is a place where many sisters must recognize that they too have a function in
the body of Christ.
Can it be said of you if you are a woman, one who is converted in a child of God, if
your name is in the book of life?
Can it be said about you as it says here in Philippians 4.3, that you have shared in
the struggle for the gospel, seeking to remain in submission to a man and yet sharing in
the struggle of the gospel without giving up that meek and quiet spirit, which is of
great value in God's eyes?
Here is something that women are called to exercise a ministry in, to serve the Lord
in the spirit of the gospel, in the areas where God has opened doors for them to prophesy
and to build a church and to seek to work together in submission with those whom God
has placed above you in the Lord and to work in harmony with those who are your co-workers
in the spread of the gospel.
We turn now to Philippians 4 and verse 4.
Rejoice in the Lord always.
Again, I will say rejoice.
Let your forbearing spirit be known to all men.
The Lord is near.
Be anxious for nothing, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving,
let your requests be made known to God.
And the peace of God which surpasses all comprehension shall guard your hearts and
your minds in Christ Jesus.
Now here are three things that Paul speaks of in these verses.
First of all, joy.
This is a fruit of the Spirit.
We read in Galatians 5.22, the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, and
so on.
And he speaks here about joy, peace, and patience.
These fruits of the Spirit mentioned in Galatians 5.22.
First of all, joy in verse 4.
Then about patience in verse 5.
Let your patience or your long suffering or forbearing nature be known to all men.
And then he speaks about peace in verse 6 and 7.
Now these are things that should be found in our life along with righteousness and love.
For the fruit of the Spirit is love, and along with that love, joy, peace, and patience.
The kingdom of God we are told in Romans 14.17 is righteousness, and along with that righteousness,
peace and joy in the Holy Spirit.
Joy is an essential characteristic of the Christian life.
Rejoice in the Lord always.
When it says always, it means always.
And again he says in verse 4, rejoice.
There is absolutely no excuse for not rejoicing always.
Deep down in our heart there must be a perpetual joy.
Now this is something which is part of the kingdom of God as we have seen in Romans
That our kingdom, the kingdom into which we enter when we surrender our life to the Lord
and are baptized and filled with the Holy Spirit, is a kingdom of righteousness, peace,
and joy in the Holy Spirit.
It is something that Christians cannot experience without the power of the Holy Spirit.
It is something that Old Testament saints could never experience because the Spirit
had not come to indwell man in those days.
It's joy that comes through the Holy Spirit as we saw in Romans 14.17.
But now that the Spirit has come, we can rejoice always.
Elijah we read in 1 Kings chapter 18 and 19, ran away from Jezebel the Queen and sat depressed
under a juniper tree asking God to take away his life.
He certainly didn't have joy at that time.
But that's no excuse for ours being depressed today.
For now we can be filled with the Holy Spirit within and have joy in the Holy Spirit all
the time.
If we are willing to take the cross and die to ourselves every day, die to seeking our
own pleasure and our own satisfaction, then we can rejoice always, no matter what other
people do.
Jesus said that the water that He would give, He told the Samaritan woman, would be like
a spring of water within that would be constantly bubbling up.
Now there's a lot of difference between having a spring of water in your own compound,
a well of water or a spring of water, and having a tap water that comes from the municipal
corporation.
The water that comes through the tap from the corporation can be cut off when they turn
off the water supply.
But the water that comes from the spring in your own compound can never be cut off.
And the joy that God gives us is not something that can be turned off by somebody else.
It can never be turned off because it's the Holy Spirit welling up within our hearts.
Ask yourself this question, can someone else take away your joy?
Because if someone says something to you or about you, or you heard somebody having
said something about you, or somebody does something to hurt you or to offend you, if
it takes away your joy, then it is obvious that your joy can be controlled by someone
outside of you.
But Jesus said, your joy, John 16, no man can take away from you.
And the joy of the kingdom of God is a joy that no one can take away from us because
it is a joy that is found in God Himself.
We read in Romans in chapter 5 of three types of joy.
First of all, in Romans 5, we read, we rejoice because of this grace in which we stand.
Romans 5 verse 2, we have obtained introduction by faith into this grace in which we stand,
and we exalt in hope of the glory of God.
The hope that we can share the glory of God and that God has brought us into a grace is
something that brings great joy to us, and that's right.
But then a stage further, verse 3, Romans 5, 3 is to rejoice in tribulation because
that glory can be ours only as we go through tribulation and testing and are faithful in
it.
So it's a further stage when we can rejoice not only in the grace in which we stand, in
the hope of the glory of God, but also in tribulations through which we can partake
of the divine nature.
But it doesn't stop there.
In verse 11 of Romans 5, we read of a higher degree of joy, and that is rejoicing in
God Himself.
And that is how our joy is purified, not in what God has done for us or is going to do
for us, not even in the fact that we are going to partake of the divine nature.
All this is legitimate joy, but the highest form of joy is to joy in God Himself.
And that's what we read in Philippians 4, 4, rejoice, not in the grace in which we
stand, not in tribulations, which are all legitimate, but in the Lord.
And it is only in the Lord that we can rejoice always if we find our joy in God.
In the Old Testament, we read in the book of Habakkuk, and chapter 3 in verses 17 to
19, he says that although the fit tree doesn't blossom, there's no fruit in the
vines, the yield of the olive fails, the feeds produce no food, the flock cut off from
the fold, there's no cattle in the stalls, yet I will rejoice in the Lord, I will
rejoice in the God of my salvation.
He says, everything around me is collapsed, my farms have produced no food, the flock has
